Mastery experience in the logs
NTI Uppsala TE22 + TE23 · CMU CS Academy logs · checked on te24c

Mastery experience in the logs

Which traces of practice in programming log data go with programming self-efficacy, and what do they say about the sources and effects of self-efficacy that social cognitive theory names? Self-efficacy (15 items, Steinhorst et al. 2020, n = 93) was measured once, in May–June 2025, at the end of TE23’s course and about eleven months after TE22’s. It is predicted from 70 log features in 9 families, each placed in social cognitive theory. The features are computed for stretches of the curriculum, whole units and the sections inside them, following book ch. 7 (Saqr & López-Pernas 2024): compute the features for a window, fit a random forest, then move the window.

What the analysis found

Students modelled9362 TE22 · 31 TE23 · 153 with logs
Full-course R².20random forest, raw features, 10×10 CV
Best window R².22sections 3.2–12.1 · units 4–7 .22
High vs Low AUC.78best window · full course .77
Earliest at R² .15Units 1–5sections 1.1–5.1 · about week 13
A new class (te24c)ρ .41units 1–4, n = 22; level, not change
  • The logs carry a real but modest signal. Over the full course the random forest explains 20% of the variance in self-efficacy (cross-validated R² .195, Spearman ρ .45), and the best windows about 22%. It separates High from Low with AUC up to .78. Every model put through a permutation test beat all 100 label-shuffled runs (p = .01). Of 64 corrected t-tests against the mean baseline, 40 give p < .05 and 10 survive Holm correction.
  • Units and sections perform alike. The best section window (sections 3.2–12.1, R² .220) and the best unit window (units 4–7, .218) do not differ (corrected t-test, two-sided p = .97). Sections place the signal more finely in the curriculum.
  • Nothing in unit 1, then two steps. Unit 1 alone gives R² .039 in the re-check (p = .22). Forward section windows stay low through unit 1 (R² ≤ .07) and take a first step once most of unit 2 is in (sections 1.1–2.3: .13). The second step comes around units 4–5: sections 1.1–5.1 is the first section window to reach R² .15, and units 1–5 the first unit window (.206 in the re-check; the classes had done most of unit 5 by about week 13). After that the curves level off (median R² .18, up to .22).
  • Leaving out the first units helps, as in version 1. The best backward windows, units 3–11 (R² .216) and sections 3.2–12.1 (.220), beat the full course. The early units, which everyone works through actively, mostly add noise.
  • What goes with high self-efficacy fits social cognitive theory. The strongest correlates are mastery experience (point completion (ρ .46): finishing what one attempts), persistence (error quotient (ρ −.45), recovery at the next run (ρ .42)), self-regulation (sessions (ρ .44), work outside lessons (ρ .40), start latency (ρ −.39)) and standing among peers (standing in the class (ρ .44)). 38 of 70 features pass FDR correction; none of the trajectory features does. Presence in lessons goes with neither (attendance ρ .07): what counts is the work students do between lessons.
  • Self-efficacy is not the grade. Sessions per active day (.43 against .28 with the grade), the error quotient (−.45 against −.35) and runs ending in an error (−.41 against −.28) go more with the belief. The amount of work (file edits .37 against .56, points completed .44 against .60) and the final project’s code go more with the grade.
  • It carries over to a new class. Models trained on TE22/TE23 and applied to te24c’s first four units (another teacher, another year) rank te24c’s after-course self-efficacy with a median ρ of .41 over the forward section windows (n = 22). They do not predict the change from before the course (median ρ .13, n = 16).

Self-efficacy was measured once, after the course; TE22 answered about eleven months after theirs ended. Social cognitive theory expects both directions here: mastery experience builds self-efficacy, and self-efficacy shapes which tasks students take on, how hard they work and how long they persist. These are associations with a later self-report, not effects, and an “early” window predicts an end-of-course state, not a future change.

The features and social cognitive theory

Every feature family has a place in social cognitive theory (Bandura 1986, 1997), with self-regulation in its socio-cognitive form (Zimmerman 2000). Named means the theory names the link between the construct and self-efficacy. Reading means the construct is the theory’s but tying these log measures to it is our interpretation.

FamilyWhat it stands for in the theoryBasisFeaturesq < .05Strongest (ρ with self-efficacy)
Mastery experiencethe first source of self-efficacy: succeeding at tasks, most of all after effort; choosing challenging tasksnamed1410Point completion (.46)
Persistence and debuggingpersistence when things go wrong (an effect of self-efficacy); failure as negative mastery experience; error streaks as affective statesnamed; streaks a reading136Error quotient (−.45)
Self-regulationtime management and structured practice (the performance phase), planning and pacing (forethought); the lessons as the settingnamed (self-regulated learning); the log proxies a reading2311Sessions (.44)
Efforthow much effort people spend (an effect of self-efficacy)named54File edits (.37)
Social comparisonvicarious experience: judging one’s capability against peersnamed; the log proxies a reading22Standing in the class (.44)
Lesson questionsmastery experience in low-stakes checks and monitoring one’s understanding; very fast answers as withdrawn effortreading21Lesson questions right at the first try (.39)
Work strategytask strategies in the performance phasereading42Variety of event types (−.41)
Trajectoryreciprocal causation over the course; self-reflection adapting later practicereading30Completion-rate trend (.21)
Creative workmastery experience in open-ended tasks; setting one’s own challengereading42Decisions in the final project (.39)

Verbal persuasion and physiological states, two of the four sources of self-efficacy, leave no trace in these logs. Vicarious experience appears only as standing: the logs show where a student stood in the class, not whether they compared themselves with anyone. Outcome expectations, the other belief the theory puts next to self-efficacy, have no direct log trace either.

How the features were chosen. Version 1 of this chapter used all 118 features of its dictionary. For this version (October 2026) they were revised. Near-copies and features that went with nothing were dropped (46 kept). 24 new features were added where exploratory analyses of the same students showed that they go with self-efficacy or the grade, and only where they fit social cognitive theory. Those analyses are chapters 3, 6, 7 and 13, and the exploratory checks of Chapter 15. The numbers on this page therefore describe how well these features do in these students. They are not an independent test. The te24c check at the end is the out-of-sample part.

How it was set up

The decisions that matter for reading the charts.

Data and target

2.25 million events from 153 students, each cohort’s own course year (TE22 2023/24, TE23 2024/25, with TE23 cut at their survey time). Students who declined the use of their CS Academy data are left out, and survey answers are used only where the student consented. Blur, resize and auto-reload events are excluded because they were logged in one year only. Self-efficacy is the mean of the answered items (at least 12 of 15): α = .96, ω = .96, and one dominant factor (eigenvalue 9.9, next 1.05). High/Low is a median split at 5.27, as in book ch. 7.

Units and sections

Windows are stretches of the curriculum, the same material for every student whatever their pace. Units 1–11 (unit 11 includes unit 12 and the final project) and their 77 sections (1.1 … 12.1, a median of 6 exercises each). An exercise belongs to its section by its number. A lesson page takes its section from a map of lesson pages to sections, built from when the five classes completed them (97% of lesson-page events). 85% of events have a section; the rest are sandbox, navigation and other courses. 66 unit windows (forward, backward, rolling 2–5 units, single) and 229 section windows (forward, backward, single). Version 1 also compared teaching weeks. A week holds different content for fast and slow students, so week windows mix what students practised with their pace, and they are dropped here. Pace has its own chapter (Chapter 13) and enters here as features: lead over the class and start latency.

Features and factors

70 features in 9 families, recomputed from the events of each window. A few exist only for the whole course: the creative tasks, the final project’s code and its last week. Sessions break after 30 minutes without events, and active time counts gaps of up to 5 minutes. Lessons are each class’s own lesson times, detected from co-activity. Within each family a factor analysis (rank-normal input, parallel analysis, minres with varimax) is fitted on all 153 logged students without the outcome. It gives 17 factors for the full course. No two features correlate at |r| ≥ .98.

Models and validation

Random forest (default mtry), an elastic net or L2-logistic baseline, and a mean baseline. Each is fitted on raw features (with book ch. 7’s |r| > .75 filter) and on family factors. Validation is repeated stratified 10-fold CV: 3 repeats for all 295 windows, and 10 repeats on fresh splits with 500 trees for the 8 key windows. The key windows also get corrected t-tests, permutation tests and cohort transfer. Last, the models are applied to a class they never saw (te24c).

Model Metric

Forward: growing windows from the course start

Each point is a model trained on everything from section 1.1 up to that point. The axis is the curriculum: the 77 sections in order, with a tick where each unit starts. Unit windows sit at their last section. Both lines end in the full course. Shaded bands show ±1 SD across CV repeats. The values behind all window charts, for every model and metric, are in one file: self-efficacy-windows.csv (2,950 windows × models).

Story thread · When it shows

In their first week, three in four students are in the most active weekly state, and who ends the year in the top half for exercises passed can already be predicted from two weeks of activity (AUC .82; Chapter 3, prediction). Self-efficacy cannot: unit 1 carries nothing, here and in te24c. Early activity is high and alike; the differences that go with the belief build up later, as students finish, stall or fall behind (Chapter 4).

Key windows, re-checked

The full course, the best window of each scheme, the earliest forward unit and section windows to reach R² .15 in the curves, and unit 1. Each was re-run with 10×10-fold CV on fresh splits and 500 trees, so the selection and the evaluation don’t share splits. The p-value is the one-sided corrected resampled t-test (Nadeau–Bengio) of the random forest against the mean baseline, using the better feature set, before and after Holm correction over all 64 model-versus-baseline tests; ρ is the random forest’s, with the same set. Permutation tests

Labels shuffled 100 times and the whole CV pipeline re-run each time. Observed R² comes from one 10-fold split, which is why it differs slightly from the table above.

Does it transfer across cohorts?

Trained on one cohort only and tested on the other. The rank correlation in the test cohort is the fairest measure here, because R² also penalises the cohorts’ different means and spreads. Each cell is Spearman ρ in the held-out cohort (→ TE23 means trained on TE22). Green marks ρ ≥ .30. For the random forest the median is .35 (range .03 to .53).

Robustness (full course). Refitting the factor analysis inside each training fold, instead of once on all logged students, changes random forest R² from .138 to .128 and elastic net from .193 to .179. The pooled fit was at most slightly optimistic. Tuning mtry by out-of-bag error, as book ch. 7 does, gives .212 against .214 with the default (raw features).

What goes with high self-efficacy

Spearman correlations of within-class ranks, pooled over the five classes, between the full-course family factors and self-efficacy. Coloured bars pass FDR correction (q < .05). Hover a bar for the interval, the per-cohort values and the correlation with the final grade.

Strongest single features

Full course, with 95% bootstrap intervals and FDR over all 70 features. The grade column is the same correlation with the final grade, as a check: features that go with both are more than a quirk of the survey.

Story thread · Improves

This speaks to a puzzle in the Log atlas, where the pass rate of graded submissions was unrelated to self-efficacy (ρ .03) and controlling for exercise points was proposed as the test (Chapter 3). Point completion, the share of the points of the exercises a student attempted that they went on to solve, is close to that test, and it is the strongest correlate here (ρ .46): finishing counts, however many tries it takes. Recovering from an error on the next run (ρ .42) is the same idea at the scale of seconds; Chapter 6 shows which errors students learn to recover from faster.

Two exploratory checks behind these features. Choosing harder exercises (ρ .36 here) still goes with self-efficacy when the amount of work and the Year 1 block/text test are held constant (ρ .30, n = 80). The checkpoints that introduce events, nested conditionals and step events mark where a new concept is hard: the minutes on them go with lower self-efficacy (ρ −.31 to −.36). Both are on Chapter 15, with the other checks.

Which families the forest relies on as the course unfolds

Share of random forest importance (raw features, forward section windows, the last column the full course) by family. Impurity importance is noisy at n = 93, and a family with more features tends to get a larger share, so read the broad pattern rather than individual cells. Over the full course the largest shares are self-regulation (29%), mastery experience (26%), persistence and debugging (18%).

A new class: te24c

te24c (2025/26, Teacher 3) answered the same survey before and after its course, and its logs cover units 1–4. The models were trained on TE22/TE23 for each forward window within units 1–4 and applied to te24c’s logs, with te24c’s own consent rules. With 22 students (16 with both surveys), it is a direction check, not a test.

Self-efficacy after the course

Change from before the course

The level carries over. Over the 29 forward section windows the random forest’s predictions rank te24c’s after-course self-efficacy with a median ρ of .41 (interquartile range .27–.51; elastic net .40), and unit 1 alone gives nothing (−.06), as in TE22/TE23. The change is not predicted (median ρ .13 and .03; with the before score held constant .08 and .00), and windows that include unit 4 go the wrong way. What the logs say about self-efficacy here is mostly where a student stands, not where they are heading.

Factor analysis by family

Full-course solution, each factor named by its highest loadings. Stability φ is Tucker’s congruence between each window’s factors and the full-course factors, median over the forward and backward windows of 3 units or 20 sections or longer. Values ≥ .85 count as similar, ≥ .95 as equal. KMO below .6 means a family barely factors; with two features (social comparison, lesson questions) the KMO is .50 by construction.

Caveats

  • With n = 93 every estimate is wide. The window curves compare 295 windows, so their peaks are optimistic. Fresh splits reduce that for the key windows but don’t remove it, because the students are the same.
  • The features were chosen with the same students’ exploratory results in view (see “How the features were chosen”). A better fit than version 1’s is therefore expected and is not evidence on its own.
  • TE22 answered the survey a year after their course. Pooling assumes the log–self-efficacy relation is similar across cohorts; the cohort-transfer check and te24c support that.
  • The 15-item scale leaves out the 5 OOP and recursion items of the published 20-item instrument. It is reliable here (α = .96) but not validated in this form.
  • Section windows depend on content attribution: lesson pages are placed by a map built from completion times, and 15% of events (sandbox, navigation) belong to no section.

What this means

  • When to look. For early warning, units 1–5 or sections 1.1–5.1 are the earliest windows that carry the signal; unit 1 carries nothing. For explanation, the course from unit 3 on, or the full course, carries the most.
  • What to look at. Finishing what one attempts, getting past errors, coming back between lessons and keeping up with the class go with higher self-efficacy. Presence in lessons does not.
  • How to use the factors. The 17 full-course family factors come close to the raw features (mean R² .103 against .121 over all windows, never significantly different) and are named in social cognitive theory’s terms. Chapter 5 clusters students on the factors of this chapter’s first version, before the features were revised.
All metrics are cross-validated out-of-fold values. Students who declined the use of their CS Academy data are left out, with survey answers used only where the student consented. Every window result is in self-efficacy-windows.csv.
